1.pericope_label: And these are the countries which the children of Israel inherited in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes of the children of Israel, distributed for inheritance to them. By lot was their inheritance, as the LORD commanded by the hand of Moses, for the nine tribes, and for the half tribe. For Moses had given the inheritance of two tribes and an half tribe on the other side Jordan: but unto the Levites he gave none inheritance among them. For the children of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim: therefore they gave no part unto the Levites in the land, save cities to dwell in, with their suburbs for their cattle and for their substance. As the LORD commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did, and they divided the land.

schools.summary: Press the lot as an act of providence rather than of chance, and refuse to let the human administrators be reduced to bystanders. Gill lists the ends the lot served — peace among the tribes, the vindication of Jacob’s and Moses’ predictions, and proof that the settlement was God’s and not a private arrangement — and reads Canaan itself as a type of the inheritance the saints obtain in Christ. Calvin distinguishes two operations: the lot fixed which district fell to which tribe, and the appointed men afterwards measured each district against the tribe’s numbers, so that both statements in the text are true at once. He also takes the third mention of the Levites as the point where God claims them as his own portion and puts one of Joseph’s families in their place.

Henry frames the division as the purpose of the conquest rather than its epilogue: a land subdued and left empty would have been subdued in vain. He reads the arrangements as safeguards for contentment — each tribe represented among the distributors, the two and a half already settled held to a choice made without power of revocation, Levi deliberately kept clear of entanglement in the affairs of this life. On the lot he is devotional as well as historical: its disposal is of the LORD, it was used as a solemn appeal by consent of parties, and it teaches men to believe God fitter to choose their inheritance than they are themselves.

Attend to the administrative detail and let it carry the argument. Clarke accounts for the order of the names by the nature of each office, explains why Reuben and Gad supplied no prince, and gathers the evidence that each tribe landed precisely where the two dying prophecies had placed it. He also keeps the timetable honest: the work began at Gilgal and finished at Shiloh, and cannot have been quick. Wesley credits Eleazar with the best grasp of the governing law, allows for replacements among the twelve heads where death had thinned them, and draws the distinction Calvin labours over — the lot settled the portions, not the boundaries.

Work the numbers and the sources. Keil sets out the apparent shortfall — two and a half, plus Levi, plus eight and a half would make twelve — and resolves it by Jacob’s adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh, then notes the compensation actually made to Levi in towns and pasture drawn from the other tribes. Ellicott argues that the run of clauses can only be establishing a total of twelve territorial inheritances, and supports it from the high priest’s vestments, where the shoulder-stones and the breastplate use two different reckonings of Jacob’s sons, each yielding twelve, so that the whole nation might be represented.

debates: Whether the land was divided by the lot or by the men who administered it, and how both statements can stand.
How many princes acted, and whether Joshua and Eleazar are to be counted among them.
Whether the lot fixed the boundaries of each tribe or only which district fell to it.
outliers: Clarke observes that no prince was drawn from Reuben or Gad, since those tribes had nothing at stake in a division west of Jordan.
Henry suggests the two and a half already settled may by now have regretted their choice, and holds that they had made their election without power of revocation.
Calvin argues that suspicion of the ten would have been impious, because they were named by the voice of God rather than by the votes of men.
Gill reads the whole distribution typologically, with Canaan as the heavenly inheritance and Joshua as the figure of Christ.
themes: The land divided by lot
Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the fathers
Levi given cities and not a portion
Joseph reckoned as two tribes
Providence in the fall of the lot

6.pericope_label: Then the children of Judah came unto Joshua in Gilgal: and Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite said unto him, Thou knowest the thing that the LORD said unto Moses the man of God concerning me and thee in Kadeshbarnea. Forty years old was I when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadeshbarnea to espy out the land; and I brought him word again as it was in mine heart. Nevertheless my brethren that went up with me made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD my God. And Moses sware on that day, saying, Surely the land whereon thy feet have trodden shall be thine inheritance, and thy children's for ever, because thou hast wholly followed the LORD my God.

schools.summary: Calvin reads the whole episode as a deliberate interruption of the survey: Caleb asks while the war is still hot, not for cleared ground but for permission to win it, and asks only that the reward of his labour be secured against the common lot. He defends the apparent immodesty as a necessary answer to envy, insists that the heart in the phrase means sincerity opposed to deceitful words, and refuses to speculate about the Kenezite surname. Gill fills in the setting — the deputation from Judah as the tribe’s chief men honouring their prince, the twelve spies chosen one to a tribe and in the prime of their powers, and the oath as the LORD’s own though Moses spoke it.

Henry treats Caleb’s standing as the key to the request. He was the oldest man in Israel except Joshua and twenty years older than any other, since everyone over twenty in his fortieth year had died in the wilderness; and where God has already declared his mind, referring the matter back to the lot would be a needless appeal. He defends the self-commendation on the ground that God had first pronounced it, so that Caleb repeating it is like a believer telling others what God has done for his soul; and he suggests the Kenezite title may be a name won in victory rather than a name inherited.

Clarke works the genealogy: Kenaz was more probably Jephunneh’s father than Caleb’s, but the name evidently ran in the house, since Othniel and a grandson of Caleb both bear it, and the Chronicler’s ancestry is descent rather than parentage. He then presses the harder point, that no promise of Hebron appears in the passages Caleb seems to be citing, while still judging that the trodden ground means Hebron. Wesley reads the scene administratively — the consultation had begun but the dividing had not — explains the tribe’s presence as consent freely given, and calls the self-commendation justifiable because it was the ground of the petition.

Keil settles the small questions and then raises a large one. My brethren means the other spies with Joshua excepted, since Joshua is the man addressed; and Caleb had been moved neither by the exaggerated report nor by the crowd’s threats. But the oath he cites is not in the record, and the oath that is there concerns Canaan at large rather than Hebron, so a special promise must have been made and not written down. Ellicott defends Caleb against the charge of self-seeking by observing what he asked for, and mines the two ages in the speech for the only chronology of the war we possess, arriving at seven years.

debates: Whether the oath Caleb cites is the one recorded at Kadesh-barnea, or a separate promise the narrative omits.
Whether the land his feet had trodden means Hebron specifically.
How long the conquest lasted before the division began.
Why Caleb is called the Kenezite.
Whether Caleb’s account of his own fidelity is immodest.
outliers: Ellicott sets Caleb’s haste beside Joshua’s delay and reads the two as a study in character rather than a difference of privilege.
Calvin frankly admits he cannot account for the Kenezite surname.
Henry compares the title to the Roman practice of naming a general after the country he subdued.
Clarke notes that the Chronicler’s calling Caleb a son of Hezron cannot be literal, since Hezron entered Egypt long before Caleb was born.
Gill observes that though Moses uttered the oath, it was the LORD who swore in it.
themes: Caleb comes with the children of Judah
The report brought back as it was in his heart
I wholly followed the LORD my God
The spies who made the heart of the people melt
The oath sworn at Kadesh-barnea

10.pericope_label: And now, behold, the LORD hath kept me alive, as he said, these forty and five years, even since the LORD spake this word unto Moses, while the children of Israel wandered in the wilderness: and now, lo, I am this day fourscore and five years old. As yet I am as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me: as my strength was then, even so is my strength now, for war, both to go out, and to come in. Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said.

schools.summary: Calvin gives the long life a purpose — not simply a mercy but the means by which Caleb receives what his whole generation forfeited — and reads the strength as a soldier’s as well as a general’s, with going out and coming in standing for the discharge of every duty. On the conditional he is emphatic: it is not Caleb’s doubt but a concession to what other men feel when they look at the giants, framed so that Joshua and the princes could grant a request that cost them only a hard war; the following clause, that he will drive them out as the LORD said, settles the matter. Gill traces the preservation to the terms of the promise and marvels at mind and body alike unimpaired while a generation fell in the wilderness.

Henry divides the forty-five years by their perils, the desert and then the war, and draws the lesson that a life so kept is owed back in praise. He treats the unabated strength as the promise outdone, since God gives more than he undertakes to give, and reads the hesitancy of the conditional as humility, not distrust: Caleb had spoken confidently of God being with Israel, and speaks warily only of his own unworthiness, resting on God’s presence rather than on his valour, his tribe, or Joshua’s aid. He ends on Caleb’s motive for choosing occupied ground — to prize a promise above a providence, and to shame his brethren forward.

Wesley does the arithmetic, thirty-eight years and then seven, and insists that the strength claimed is for marching and fighting rather than counsel, so that the grant is not wasted; Moses had said that at eighty strength is labour and sorrow, and Caleb is the exception, which he owes to following the LORD fully. He also explains why a country and not a city is asked for, the cities being destined for the Levites, and takes the conditional as godly fear about his own particular enterprise rather than about the nation’s war. Clarke voices the same energy from another side — the request is not for a place of retirement but for a fight — and argues that since Hebron had already fallen, what is sought is the surrounding country still held in force.

Keil identifies the mountain from the context as the highland about Hebron where the spies encountered the Anakim, and reads the two clauses of the petition as co-ordinate rather than dependent. Ellicott takes up the comparison the verse provokes: the same book says Joshua had aged, though he outlived this scene and died at a hundred and ten, only twenty-five years Caleb’s senior. Rather than treat it as a discrepancy he explains it from circumstance — the weight of command lay on Joshua and not on Caleb, and temperament may have done the rest.

debates: What the conditional if so be expresses: doubt of God, humility about oneself, or the difficulty of the task as other men see it.
Whether this mountain means Hebron, or the hill country around it.
Whether Hebron had been retaken by its old inhabitants after Joshua captured it.
Why Joshua had aged while Caleb had not.
outliers: Calvin observes that the difficulty of the work is measured by the delay: Joshua was dead before Caleb attacked the giants.
Clarke reports and then sets aside the conjecture that the Anakim slipped back into Hebron while the army was campaigning elsewhere.
Wesley points out that the cities of this district were afterwards assigned to the Levites, which is why Caleb asks for the country.
Ellicott resolves the two men’s different ageing by the weight of office rather than by any difference of grace.
Henry holds that Caleb chose occupied ground deliberately, as a spur to the tribes still to fight for theirs.
themes: The LORD hath kept me alive these forty and five years
Strength for war, to go out and to come in
Give me this mountain
The Anakims and their great fenced cities
If so be the LORD will be with me

13.pericope_label: And Joshua blessed him, and gave unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh Hebron for an inheritance. Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel. And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war.

schools.summary: Calvin treats the blessing as a public act: Joshua’s warmth was meant to be seen, since praising this valour was itself an exhortation to a people still afraid of the giants. He then presses the one legal problem in the chapter — Hebron is later a Levitical city and a city of refuge, yet Caleb is named its owner — and after offering the solution that the Levites held only a right of residence, honestly abandons it for the harder reading, that their title was full and that a distribution by lot wronged nobody. He also rejects the tradition that the city of four commemorates four patriarchs buried there. Gill takes the blessing as grant, congratulation and prayer at once, and lays out four rival derivations of Kirjath-arba without settling on one.
Henry marks that the grant was to Caleb and his heirs, and that the text supplies its own reason for it in his having wholly followed the LORD God of Israel — singular piety meeting singular favour.

Clarke reads the blessing partly as commendation, since to bless is often simply to speak well of a man, and stresses the legal form of what followed: a conveyance made before the elders, publicly acknowledged, and so exempt from the lot. On the old name he argues for four Anakim, probably brothers, while admitting that the next chapter treats Arba as a personal name, and he derives Hebron from a root meaning to associate. He also gives the closing clause a precise sense: not that fighting ceased, but that general campaigns did, leaving each tribe its own remaining enemies. Wesley keeps the blessing to prayer, and takes the great man as great in stature, strength and authority alike.

Keil explains why the city is named when the mountain was asked for — Hebron is the chief town of the district, which included Debir — and dates the notes about the older name to the writer’s own day, so that the disuse of Kirjath-arba proves nothing about which name is older. He also reads the repeated rest from war as an assurance that the surviving Anakim did not delay the distribution. Ellicott is confident that Arba is a personal name, weighs whether Hebron or Kirjath-arba came first without forcing a decision, corrects the great man to the great man, and frankly finds the closing clause easier to account for at the end of the war narrative than here.

debates: What Joshua’s blessing consisted of: prayer, commendation, or the grant itself.
Whether Kirjath-arba means the city of four or the city of a man named Arba.
Whether Hebron or Kirjath-arba is the older name.
How Caleb’s ownership of Hebron squares with its later status as a Levitical city and city of refuge.
Why the notice that the land had rest from war stands here as well as at the end of the war narrative.
outliers: Calvin observes that Caleb cannot have been seeking present ease, since he did not take possession until many years later.
Calvin advances the theory that the Levites held only a right of residence and then withdraws it in favour of the evidence against him.
Clarke dismisses the four-patriarchs derivation on the ground that such traditions confute themselves.
Clarke notes that the Septuagint styles Hebron the metropolis of the Anakim.
Gill preserves a tradition that Hebron was named from a descendant of Caleb, which would make the name here an anticipation.
themes: Joshua blessed him
Hebron given for an inheritance
Because he wholly followed the LORD
Kirjath-arba and the sons of Anak
The land had rest from war
